b: I. Everything In Its Right Place

Everything is in its right place: gleaming, polished surfaces and crisp, filtered museum air. I peer into a large glass vitrine displaying a handful of woven baskets. One delicate and spiky as a sea urchin, with vertical brown and gold stripes. Another, about the size of an acorn squash, blonde and radiating iridescent blue points.

More cases around the gallery feature other shapes and styles: taller vaselike forms; wider, bowl-shaped baskets; arrays of vertical, horizontal, and diagonal patterns wrapping around curves; beaded baskets; basket lids stippled with dyed porcupine quills depicting loons and other animals. I lean in and take a closer look, marveling at the progression from one object to the next, as if each basket suggests the next answer in a long and complex numerical sequence. Same logic, different result.

From the back of the gallery, I hear the gentle, beckoning sounds of birds in a forest, then the workmanlike hum of a distant chainsaw, then a slow, methodic pounding. The exhibition of baskets is still and clear but for these distant sounds and the bright digital motion of a video projection in the back of the room. Briefly, an image of flames—something on fire—catches my eye.

I encountered “Ash,” a film by the artist Jeremy Frey at the Art Institute of Chicago (AIC) as part of Frey’s solo exhibition Woven. I teach anthropology and ethnography classes across the street from the AIC at the School of the Art Institute, and I often wander over with my students to think with them about the museum’s exhibitions and how they are entangled in the history of anthropology, which is to say, the history of colonialism and empire. To get to Woven, I had to navigate a labyrinth of hallways and galleries: a long corridor of South Asian artifacts (jewelry, Hindu gods, smiling Buddhas), then down a set of stairs past the dark, moody Egypt galleries (jewelry, sarcophagi, scarabs behind glass), finally entering a brightly lit gallery filled with Frey’s work.

On arriving to the gallery, I had that feeling that I so often get in museum exhibitions—of everything being in its right place, a sense of serene order, timelessness, stillness. Frey, a Passamaquoddy artist based in Maine, is known for his handmade baskets, which emerge out of a centuries-old Indigenous tradition that has been called “the oldest art form in New England,”1 and the gallery was filled with glass vitrines displaying Frey’s baskets. These displays instilled a sense of sequential order. As curator Andrew James Hamilton writes, “Every basket he weaves is a reaction to one that came before: a next step, an alternate approach, or a doubling down.”2 Works from Frey’s expanded repertoire of prints and sculptures hung on the wall, everything framed and orderly.

Frey’s work is often understood as living on the threshold between “traditional” and “innovative,” and many have commented on Frey’s position as a Native artist working within these categorical contradictions. But there is a deeper concern that surfaces in “Ash,” one which points toward the connections between the settler colonial project of Native dispossession—of land, of objects, of life—and the art museum—its modes of display, its categories of presentation, and its complicity in the destruction of the earth. In this context, “Ash” offers a radical decolonial critique of artmaking and art presentation.
I felt my position shifting from observer of “process” to observer of “art,” admiring the object on the screen in front of me devoid of context, pure aesthetics.

The first time I saw the film, projected against a back wall of the gallery, I arrived at an image of Frey—a muscular man in a blue T-shirt, blue jeans, and hiking boots—aggressively whacking the side of a log in his driveway with the flat side of a wood axe. The video then cut to Frey peeling away strips of wood from the log (presumably shaken loose from the pounding), stacking them together, and bundling them. It cuts again to Frey in his workshop, cluttered with carpentry tools, raw materials, and half-finished baskets, processing the wood down into weaveable strips, some of which are transferred to a pot on a stovetop filled with bubbling blue liquid.

At this point my body caught the rhythm of the film, and I sank into the familiar experience of watching a material process unfold along a compressed timeline. Frey turns a different block of wood on a lathe and carves away at it with a sharp chisel as woodchips fly toward the camera lens. The block transforms into a vaselike shape, which he cuts on a bandsaw into four equal parts. He weaves thin strips of wood into a round base and positions them under the four blocks. He attaches vertical pieces to the base and weaves horizontal strips against them, alternating natural and dyed strips into exquisite stripes. I watched the alchemy of raw materials becoming basket as Frey removes the inner blocks one at a time, leaving the basket to stand on its own with no internal support as he weaves the final elements of the basket’s upper rim.

After finishing the basket’s lid, the film abruptly cuts to Frey in a white box gallery positioning the basket on a tall white plinth. The scene is so clearly set in the art gallery—bright, museum-quality lighting, white walls, white plinth. I felt my position shifting from observer of “process” to observer of “art,” admiring the object on the screen in front of me devoid of context, pure aesthetics. And it is beautiful: slender at the base, expanding toward the top, alternating blue, brown, and white stripes running vertically and horizontally. A basket on a white plinth in a white walled gallery, projected on a white wall in a gallery full of baskets on plinths. Everything in its right place.

Except then—as the sounds of the birds in the forest return—the basket in the video begins to smoke, then smolder. What looks like a vase of flaming flowers becomes a black smoking carcass, the basket reduced to its studs. And not only does the basket burn away, but when I situate myself at just the right angle to the video screen, with a basket between myself and the video projection, it appears that the basket in the gallery is on fire, too, the flames threatening to leap from one object to the next, igniting the gallery walls and the museum alongside it.

Here the screen goes black, providing some indication of the film’s completion. But after a brief interlude and title screen it resumes, opening with a wide view of the lush Maine woods brimming with ferns and young ash trees. Frey wanders into the frame wearing a flannel and holding a chainsaw. I watch the cycle begin again: He carefully selects a tree, fells it with the chainsaw, strips it of branches, props it up on his shoulder and lugs it away. I see him setting the log down on two braces in his driveway. He places one foot on the end of the log to steady it and begins aggressively whacking it with the flat side of an axe.
III. Process Problems and the Ethnographic Gaze

In its formal qualities, “Ash” fits neatly within what scholar Salomé Skvirsky has called “the process genre”: a category of film and media that depicts some kind of repeatable action in a “sequentially ordered series of steps with a clearly identifiable beginning, middle, and end.”3 Examples include shows like How It’s Made, which depicts the step-by-step manufacturing processes of everyday industrial objects like baseballs and manhole covers, and documentaries showcasing various cultural practices from beginning to end. Skvirsky ascribes a uniquely hypnotizing quality to these films, both in the way they compress time and space, and in the deep satisfaction we get from observing raw materials transform into finished products.

Process films, Skvirsky continues, convince us that the things we see being made in front of us are the truest versions of themselves. How It’s Made doesn’t work if the baseball turns out lopsided and irregular. We understand implicitly that the baseball is the baseball, and that its manufacturing process is shown to us as an idealized sequence of events without failure or flaw. Likewise, despite the diversity of size, shape, color, and material in the gallery all around me, I implicitly understand that the basket being made during “Ash” is not just one of Jeremy Frey’s baskets, but all of them.

Process films—particularly in their ability to support the “exemplary” status of objects—overlap with another documentary form, “ethnography,” the primary scholarly output of cultural anthropology. Ethnography—literally writing (-graphy) about people (ethno-)—emerged in the late 19th century as a way for anthropologists to document the world’s cultural diversity. Skvirsky offers the example, among others, of anthropologist Félix-Louis Regnault’s time-lapse photographs, displayed at the Exposition Ethnographique in Paris, 1895, which portrayed so-called “primitive” peoples undertaking basic production processes, such as a Wolof woman making pottery.

At the turn of the 20th century, ethnographic process films like these, almost universally created by white men about non-white people, were integral to the development of the anthropological theory of cultural evolution—the idea that all cultures evolved along the same trajectory from primitive to civilized, with Western (i.e., white) cultural production representing the most advanced. Ethnographic process films were thought to be “salvaging” Indigenous cultural processes from their demise at the hands of Western civilizational progress, plotted out in the name of science before they disappeared forever.4 What does it mean, then, that part of Frey’s process includes the basket’s incineration?

Walk about a mile south from Frey’s exhibition at the AIC to the Field Museum, and you will encounter a wholly different collection of Indigenous-made baskets and art objects. Here at the Field, whose mission is to present “science” to the public rather than “art,” Indigenous objects are housed alongside collections of meteorites, taxidermized birds, and dinosaur skeletons. Many of these objects are uncredited or anonymous, displayed largely by process and function: fishing equipment with hunting equipment, men’s ritual clothing next to women’s ritual clothing, and so on. The result is that despite their individual beauty and artistry, these different spiritual and household and creative objects appear to us as the same to one another rather than different, part of a “type” or “class” of objects rather than individual acts of aesthetic achievement.

In these galleries, too, you can encounter ethnographic process films depicting everyday Indigenous practices, such as one in which a white man narrates in stilted tones as a fisherman uses “traditional” nets and spears to procure a fresh catch. There are also mannequins representing Indigenous people themselves, frozen in the act of some process or another: here, a mannequin in a shaman’s cloak midway through a dance step, there, a mannequin dressed as a woman cooking over a hearth.

The AIC, on the other hand, seems to be of two minds in its approach to presenting creative work made outside of the canon of Western art. If you enter through the front entrance flanked by stone lions, as I did when I visited Woven, you pass through a series of galleries that are grouped by region (and by extension, ethnicity): Japan, Korea, Southeast Asia, and Egypt. Here, alongside stone Buddhas and gold and jade scarabs, Frey lives among “the arts”rather than “the artists.” Indeed, if Frey had been working in an earlier decade, say the 1960s, and his work was deemed to be both outstanding and exemplary of Passamaquoddy basketry, his work may have been collected by an elite Chicagoan and donated to the AIC’s “Primitive Art” collection, which folded together all of the art from Latin America and the Indigenous US, categorizing it as singularly locked in some kind of “primitive” time.56
Imagine … the impossible burden of satisfying all of these categories at once: an artist, a “Native,” a traditionalist, an innovator, a representative of the community, and a singular voice.

But if you enter the AIC through the modern wing (less stone, more glass), you navigate through a museum organized by innovation in style: cubism, surrealism, minimalism, modernism, abstract expressionism, etc. Here on this side of the museum, time marches progressively forward, while in the regional galleries, it appears to stand still.

In some ways the inclusion of Native artists like Frey into the museum is an attempt to repair the damage of this earlier system of categorization: The terminology has been updated, the collections are split apart by geographic area rather than folded under the category of “primitive,” and a more inclusive acquisition practice brings the work of Indigenous and African artists into the contemporary collection. In this sense, Frey’s solo exhibition as a Native artist, the museum suggests, will help salvage the museum from its colonial past, an evolutionary step along its long arc toward justice.

Imagine the conundrum for an Indigenous basketmaker and artist, offered a career opportunity to present their work in a museum show, and faced with the impossible burden of satisfying all of these categories at once: an artist, a “Native,” a traditionalist, an innovator, a representative of the community, and a singular voice, not to mention the pressure placed upon him from within the Indigenous community to represent things “as they should be,” a politically-disputed framework in its own right. One way to read “Ash,” then, is as a kind of refusal of these distinctions. Within these categorical contradictions, perhaps the most reasonable course of action—as the basket is placed on the pedestal once more—is to burn.

“Ash,” however, does not end in ash. Like many video installations, it plays on loop in the gallery, constantly repeating throughout the day. Frey renders a single tree into a basket which spontaneously combusts on a plinth in a white gallery (roll credits), then returns to the forest to find a new tree with which to begin creating a new basket.

The film establishes a clear link between the forest and gallery, and the scene of the burning basket is overlaid with the sounds of birds and rustling leaves—bridging the time and space between the basket’s demise and its inception in woods. The scenes of Frey harvesting wood by hand are more than just depictions of “traditional” process here: They place the artist in direct relationship to his surrounding environment—the woods of Maine—which produce the raw materials necessary for his art, to which he must return to continue.

And at the same time, Frey’s process—within the cyclicality of “Ash”—includes burning the very thing he makes, creating from his work a regenerative substance, ash, with which to fertilize the forest. Within the recurring confines of the film, artistic process becomes an endless loop that returns to its past rather than continually breaks away from it toward aesthetic achievement and its permanent arrival into a museum collection. Curator Ramey Mize has described this reciprocal sense of time in Frey’s work as “dendrochronological,” moving both inward and outward like the growth rings of trees.7 Tree becomes basket. Basket becomes ash. Ash fertilizes forest. New tree grows. In Frey’s process, there is no taking without also giving back.

Further reading reveals an existential threat: the emerald ash borer beetle, an invasive insect that was found in Maine in the early 2000s, and has since decimated millions of ash trees.8 Like uncontrollable wildfires spurned by rising global temperatures, the ash bore threatens to consume and eventually eliminate all of the supply of ash trees, which produce the supple, durable fibers that Frey and his lineage of Passamaquoddy basketmakers have been using for centuries. There are some processes, perhaps, which cannot be reversed.

Scholar Gerald Vizenor offers the term “survivance” to conceptualize the survival of traditions alongside the insistence of presence within Native American storytelling, under constant existential threat of erasure.9 In “Ash” the existential threat is twofold, not simply a matter of Indigenous survivance but of planetary survival: What happens if the flames jump from the basket in the video to the basket in the gallery? The perfect museum air begins to fill with smoke. No forests, no basket. No basket, no artist. No artist, no AIC.

In this way, the film seems to suggest that what should be burned are the frameworks which insist on the separation between art and the environment. Decolonial scholar Ariella Azoulay has proposed how appropriating objects from their communities of practice and environments leads to destruction: “The imperial conception of art contributes not only to the destruction of specific worlds here and there … but to the destruction of the world as a shared place that cannot and should not be appropriated, and first dissected into appropriable objects.”10 Here is a sharp warning of imminent environmental and social collapse, enabled by the ways the museum separates art from the people who make it and the worlds which support its making.

Standing with my back toward the film and facing the baskets on display, I hear birds in the trees and (at least in my head) the whirring crackle of the flames. This stillness all around me, the stillness of everything in its right place in the museum, can only be maintained through immense environmental and economic labor, requiring massive investment, often by trustees who themselves are the titans of extractive industries, dispossessors of land, pursuers of the never-ending accumulation of capital. Through “Ash,” Frey refuses to be stilled, to resolve into an object of inclusion within a paradigm whose gears still turn on the axles of colonialism and resource extraction despite its increasingly inclusive protocols.

If “Ash” is a process film, it depicts a process in which art evades capture and extraction through its own self-destruction. In that self-destruction it gives something back to land under threat. There is a radical proposal embedded here to provide art and artmaking with an alternative function: from a practice of creating separation from the world to one of creating reciprocal relations with it; from a relationality that centers value to one that centers aliveness and planetary survival. The museum might appear frozen from inside, but it is indeed burning from the outside in.
